95|/*!
96|@brief namespace for Niels Lohmann
97|@see https://github.com/nlohmann
98|@since version 1.0.0
99|*/
100|namespace nlohmann
101|{
102|
103|/*!
104|@brief unnamed namespace with internal helper functions
105|
106|This namespace collects some functions that could not be defined inside the
107|@ref basic_json class.
108|
109|@since version 2.1.0
110|*/
111|namespace detail
112|{
113|///////////////////////////
114|// JSON type enumeration //
115|///////////////////////////
116|
117|/*!
118|@brief the JSON type enumeration
119|
120|This enumeration collects the different JSON types. It is internally used to
121|distinguish the stored values, and the functions @ref basic_json::is_null(),
122|@ref basic_json::is_object(), @ref basic_json::is_array(),
123|@ref basic_json::is_string(), @ref basic_json::is_boolean(),
124|@ref basic_json::is_number() (with @ref basic_json::is_number_integer(),
125|@ref basic_json::is_number_unsigned(), and @ref basic_json::is_number_float()),
126|@ref basic_json::is_discarded(), @ref basic_json::is_primitive(), and
127|@ref basic_json::is_structured() rely on it.
128|
129|@note There are three enumeration entries (number_integer, number_unsigned, and
130|number_float), because the library distinguishes these three types for numbers:
131|@ref basic_json::number_unsigned_t is used for unsigned integers,
132|@ref basic_json::number_integer_t is used for signed integers, and
133|@ref basic_json::number_float_t is used for floating-point numbers or to
134|approximate integers which do not fit in the limits of their respective type.
135|
136|@sa @ref basic_json::basic_json(const value_t value_type) -- create a JSON
137|value with the default value for a given type
138|
139|@since version 1.0.0
140|*/
141|enum class value_t : uint8_t
142|{
143|    null,            ///< null value
144|    object,          ///< object (unordered set of name/value pairs)
145|    array,           ///< array (ordered collection of values)
146|    string,          ///< string value
147|    boolean,         ///< boolean value
148|    number_integer,  ///< number value (signed integer)
149|    number_unsigned, ///< number value (unsigned integer)
150|    number_float,    ///< number value (floating-point)
151|    discarded        ///< discarded by the the parser callback function
152|};
153|
154|/*!
155|@brief comparison operator for JSON types
156|
157|Returns an ordering that is similar to Python:
158|- order: null < boolean < number < object < array < string
159|- furthermore, each type is not smaller than itself
160|
161|@since version 1.0.0
162|*/
163|inline bool operator<(const value_t lhs, const value_t rhs) noexcept
164|{
165|    static constexpr std::array<uint8_t, 8> order = {{
166|            0, // null
167|            3, // object
168|            4, // array
169|            5, // string
170|            1, // boolean
171|            2, // integer
172|            2, // unsigned
173|            2, // float
174|        }
175|    };
176|
177|    // discarded values are not comparable
178|    if (lhs == value_t::discarded or rhs == value_t::discarded)
179|    {
180|        return false;
181|    }
182|
183|    return order[static_cast<std::size_t>(lhs)] <
184|           order[static_cast<std::size_t>(rhs)];
185|}
186|
187|
188|/////////////
189|// helpers //
190|/////////////
191|
192|// alias templates to reduce boilerplate
193|template<bool B, typename T = void>
194|using enable_if_t = typename std::enable_if<B, T>::type;
195|
196|template<typename T>
197|using uncvref_t = typename std::remove_cv<typename std::remove_reference<T>::type>::type;
198|
199|// taken from http://stackoverflow.com/a/26936864/266378
200|template<typename T>
201|using is_unscoped_enum =
202|    std::integral_constant<bool, std::is_convertible<T, int>::value and
203|    std::is_enum<T>::value>;
204|
205|/*
206|Implementation of two C++17 constructs: conjunction, negation. This is needed
207|to avoid evaluating all the traits in a condition
208|
209|For example: not std::is_same<void, T>::value and has_value_type<T>::value
210|will not compile when T = void (on MSVC at least). Whereas
211|conjunction<negation<std::is_same<void, T>>, has_value_type<T>>::value will
212|stop evaluating if negation<...>::value == false
213|
214|Please note that those constructs must be used with caution, since symbols can
215|become very long quickly (which can slow down compilation and cause MSVC
216|internal compiler errors). Only use it when you have to (see example ahead).
217|*/
218|template<class...> struct conjunction : std::true_type {};
219|template<class B1> struct conjunction<B1> : B1 {};
220|template<class B1, class... Bn>
221|struct conjunction<B1, Bn...> : std::conditional<bool(B1::value), conjunction<Bn...>, B1>::type {};
222|
223|template<class B> struct negation : std::integral_constant < bool, !B::value > {};
224|
225|// dispatch utility (taken from ranges-v3)
226|template<unsigned N> struct priority_tag : priority_tag < N - 1 > {};
227|template<> struct priority_tag<0> {};

297|struct external_constructor<value_t::array>
298|{
299|    template<typename BasicJsonType>
300|    static void construct(BasicJsonType& j, const typename BasicJsonType::array_t& arr)
301|    {
302|        j.m_type = value_t::array;
303|        j.m_value = arr;
304|        j.assert_invariant();
305|    }
306|
307|    template<typename BasicJsonType, typename CompatibleArrayType,
308|             enable_if_t<not std::is_same<CompatibleArrayType,
309|                                          typename BasicJsonType::array_t>::value,
310|                         int> = 0>
311|    static void construct(BasicJsonType& j, const CompatibleArrayType& arr)
312|    {
313|        using std::begin;
314|        using std::end;
315|        j.m_type = value_t::array;
316|        j.m_value.array = j.template create<typename BasicJsonType::array_t>(begin(arr), end(arr));
317|        j.assert_invariant();
318|    }
319|
320|    template<typename BasicJsonType>
321|    static void construct(BasicJsonType& j, const std::vector<bool>& arr)
322|    {
323|        j.m_type = value_t::array;
324|        j.m_value = value_t::array;
325|        j.m_value.array->reserve(arr.size());
326|        for (bool x : arr)
327|        {
328|            j.m_value.array->push_back(x);
329|        }
330|        j.assert_invariant();
331|    }
332|};

360|
361|////////////////////////
362|// has_/is_ functions //
363|////////////////////////
364|
365|/*!
366|@brief Helper to determine whether there's a key_type for T.
367|
368|This helper is used to tell associative containers apart from other containers
369|such as sequence containers. For instance, `std::map` passes the test as it
370|contains a `mapped_type`, whereas `std::vector` fails the test.
371|
372|@sa http://stackoverflow.com/a/7728728/266378
373|@since version 1.0.0, overworked in version 2.0.6
374|*/
375|#define NLOHMANN_JSON_HAS_HELPER(type)                                        \
376|    template<typename T> struct has_##type {                                  \
377|    private:                                                                  \
378|        template<typename U, typename = typename U::type>                     \
379|        static int detect(U &&);                                              \
380|        static void detect(...);                                              \
381|    public:                                                                   \
382|        static constexpr bool value =                                         \
383|                std::is_integral<decltype(detect(std::declval<T>()))>::value; \
384|    }
385|
386|NLOHMANN_JSON_HAS_HELPER(mapped_type);
387|NLOHMANN_JSON_HAS_HELPER(key_type);
388|NLOHMANN_JSON_HAS_HELPER(value_type);
389|NLOHMANN_JSON_HAS_HELPER(iterator);
390|
391|#undef NLOHMANN_JSON_HAS_HELPER
392|
393|
394|template<bool B, class RealType, class CompatibleObjectType>
395|struct is_compatible_object_type_impl : std::false_type {};
396|
397|template<class RealType, class CompatibleObjectType>
398|struct is_compatible_object_type_impl<true, RealType, CompatibleObjectType>
399|{
400|    static constexpr auto value =
401|        std::is_constructible<typename RealType::key_type,
402|        typename CompatibleObjectType::key_type>::value and
403|        std::is_constructible<typename RealType::mapped_type,
404|        typename CompatibleObjectType::mapped_type>::value;
405|};
406|
407|template<class BasicJsonType, class CompatibleObjectType>
408|struct is_compatible_object_type
409|{
410|    static auto constexpr value = is_compatible_object_type_impl <
411|                                  conjunction<negation<std::is_same<void, CompatibleObjectType>>,
412|                                  has_mapped_type<CompatibleObjectType>,
413|                                  has_key_type<CompatibleObjectType>>::value,
414|                                  typename BasicJsonType::object_t, CompatibleObjectType >::value;
415|};
416|
417|template<typename BasicJsonType, typename T>
418|struct is_basic_json_nested_type
419|{
420|    static auto constexpr value = std::is_same<T, typename BasicJsonType::iterator>::value or
421|                                  std::is_same<T, typename BasicJsonType::const_iterator>::value or
422|                                  std::is_same<T, typename BasicJsonType::reverse_iterator>::value or
423|                                  std::is_same<T, typename BasicJsonType::const_reverse_iterator>::value or
424|                                  std::is_same<T, typename BasicJsonType::json_pointer>::value;
425|};
426|
427|template<class BasicJsonType, class CompatibleArrayType>
428|struct is_compatible_array_type
429|{
430|    static auto constexpr value =
431|        conjunction<negation<std::is_same<void, CompatibleArrayType>>,
432|        negation<is_compatible_object_type<
433|        BasicJsonType, CompatibleArrayType>>,
434|        negation<std::is_constructible<typename BasicJsonType::string_t,
435|        CompatibleArrayType>>,
436|        negation<is_basic_json_nested_type<BasicJsonType, CompatibleArrayType>>,
437|        has_value_type<CompatibleArrayType>,
438|        has_iterator<CompatibleArrayType>>::value;
439|};

441|template<bool, typename, typename>
442|struct is_compatible_integer_type_impl : std::false_type {};
443|
444|template<typename RealIntegerType, typename CompatibleNumberIntegerType>
445|struct is_compatible_integer_type_impl<true, RealIntegerType, CompatibleNumberIntegerType>
446|{
447|    // is there an assert somewhere on overflows?
448|    using RealLimits = std::numeric_limits<RealIntegerType>;
449|    using CompatibleLimits = std::numeric_limits<CompatibleNumberIntegerType>;
450|
451|    static constexpr auto value =
452|        std::is_constructible<RealIntegerType,
453|        CompatibleNumberIntegerType>::value and
454|        CompatibleLimits::is_integer and
455|        RealLimits::is_signed == CompatibleLimits::is_signed;
456|};
457|
458|template<typename RealIntegerType, typename CompatibleNumberIntegerType>
459|struct is_compatible_integer_type
460|{
461|    static constexpr auto value =
462|        is_compatible_integer_type_impl <
463|        std::is_integral<CompatibleNumberIntegerType>::value and
464|        not std::is_same<bool, CompatibleNumberIntegerType>::value,
465|        RealIntegerType, CompatibleNumberIntegerType > ::value;
466|};

472|{

1176|    /// @name JSON value data types
1177|    /// The data types to store a JSON value. These types are derived from
1178|    /// the template arguments passed to class @ref basic_json.
1179|    /// @{
1180|
1181|    /*!
1182|    @brief a type for an object
1183|
1184|    [RFC 7159](http://rfc7159.net/rfc7159) describes JSON objects as follows:
1185|    > An object is an unordered collection of zero or more name/value pairs,
1186|    > where a name is a string and a value is a string, number, boolean, null,
1187|    > object, or array.
1188|
1189|    To store objects in C++, a type is defined by the template parameters
1190|    described below.
1191|
1192|    @tparam ObjectType  the container to store objects (e.g., `std::map` or
1193|    `std::unordered_map`)
1194|    @tparam StringType the type of the keys or names (e.g., `std::string`).
1195|    The comparison function `std::less<StringType>` is used to order elements
1196|    inside the container.
1197|    @tparam AllocatorType the allocator to use for objects (e.g.,
1198|    `std::allocator`)
1199|
1200|    #### Default type
1201|
1202|    With the default values for @a ObjectType (`std::map`), @a StringType
1203|    (`std::string`), and @a AllocatorType (`std::allocator`), the default
1204|    value for @a object_t is:
1205|
1206|    @code {.cpp}
1207|    std::map<
1208|      std::string, // key_type
1209|      basic_json, // value_type
1210|      std::less<std::string>, // key_compare
1211|      std::allocator<std::pair<const std::string, basic_json>> // allocator_type
1212|    >
1213|    @endcode
1214|
1215|    #### Behavior
1216|
1217|    The choice of @a object_t influences the behavior of the JSON class. With
1218|    the default type, objects have the following behavior:
1219|
1220|    - When all names are unique, objects will be interoperable in the sense
1221|      that all software implementations receiving that object will agree on
1222|      the name-value mappings.
1223|    - When the names within an object are not unique, later stored name/value
1224|      pairs overwrite previously stored name/value pairs, leaving the used
1225|      names unique. For instance, `{"key": 1}` and `{"key": 2, "key": 1}` will
1226|      be treated as equal and both stored as `{"key": 1}`.
1227|    - Internally, name/value pairs are stored in lexicographical order of the
1228|      names. Objects will also be serialized (see @ref dump) in this order.
1229|      For instance, `{"b": 1, "a": 2}` and `{"a": 2, "b": 1}` will be stored
1230|      and serialized as `{"a": 2, "b": 1}`.
1231|    - When comparing objects, the order of the name/value pairs is irrelevant.
1232|      This makes objects interoperable in the sense that they will not be
1233|      affected by these differences. For instance, `{"b": 1, "a": 2}` and
1234|      `{"a": 2, "b": 1}` will be treated as equal.
1235|
1236|    #### Limits
1237|
1238|    [RFC 7159](http://rfc7159.net/rfc7159) specifies:
1239|    > An implementation may set limits on the maximum depth of nesting.
1240|
1241|    In this class, the object's limit of nesting is not constraint explicitly.
1242|    However, a maximum depth of nesting may be introduced by the compiler or
1243|    runtime environment. A theoretical limit can be queried by calling the
1244|    @ref max_size function of a JSON object.
1245|
1246|    #### Storage
1247|
1248|    Objects are stored as pointers in a @ref basic_json type. That is, for any
1249|    access to object values, a pointer of type `object_t*` must be
1250|    dereferenced.
1251|
1252|    @sa @ref array_t -- type for an array value
1253|
1254|    @since version 1.0.0
1255|
1256|    @note The order name/value pairs are added to the object is *not*
1257|    preserved by the library. Therefore, iterating an object may return
1258|    name/value pairs in a different order than they were originally stored. In
1259|    fact, keys will be traversed in alphabetical order as `std::map` with
1260|    `std::less` is used by default. Please note this behavior conforms to [RFC
1261|    7159](http://rfc7159.net/rfc7159), because any order implements the
1262|    specified "unordered" nature of JSON objects.
1263|    */
1264|    using object_t = ObjectType<StringType,
1265|          basic_json,
1266|          std::less<StringType>,
1267|          AllocatorType<std::pair<const StringType,
1268|          basic_json>>>;
1269|
1270|    /*!
1271|    @brief a type for an array
1272|
1273|    [RFC 7159](http://rfc7159.net/rfc7159) describes JSON arrays as follows:
1274|    > An array is an ordered sequence of zero or more values.
1275|
1276|    To store objects in C++, a type is defined by the template parameters
1277|    explained below.
1278|
1279|    @tparam ArrayType  container type to store arrays (e.g., `std::vector` or
1280|    `std::list`)
1281|    @tparam AllocatorType allocator to use for arrays (e.g., `std::allocator`)
1282|
1283|    #### Default type
1284|
1285|    With the default values for @a ArrayType (`std::vector`) and @a
1286|    AllocatorType (`std::allocator`), the default value for @a array_t is:
1287|
1288|    @code {.cpp}
1289|    std::vector<
1290|      basic_json, // value_type
1291|      std::allocator<basic_json> // allocator_type
1292|    >
1293|    @endcode
1294|
1295|    #### Limits
1296|
1297|    [RFC 7159](http://rfc7159.net/rfc7159) specifies:
1298|    > An implementation may set limits on the maximum depth of nesting.
1299|
1300|    In this class, the array's limit of nesting is not constraint explicitly.
1301|    However, a maximum depth of nesting may be introduced by the compiler or
1302|    runtime environment. A theoretical limit can be queried by calling the
1303|    @ref max_size function of a JSON array.
1304|
1305|    #### Storage
1306|
1307|    Arrays are stored as pointers in a @ref basic_json type. That is, for any
1308|    access to array values, a pointer of type `array_t*` must be dereferenced.
1309|
1310|    @sa @ref object_t -- type for an object value
1311|
1312|    @since version 1.0.0
1313|    */
1314|    using array_t = ArrayType<basic_json, AllocatorType<basic_json>>;
1315|
1316|    /*!
1317|    @brief a type for a string
1318|
1319|    [RFC 7159](http://rfc7159.net/rfc7159) describes JSON strings as follows:
1320|    > A string is a sequence of zero or more Unicode characters.
1321|
1322|    To store objects in C++, a type is defined by the template parameter
1323|    described below. Unicode values are split by the JSON class into
1324|    byte-sized characters during deserialization.
1325|
1326|    @tparam StringType  the container to store strings (e.g., `std::string`).
1327|    Note this container is used for keys/names in objects, see @ref object_t.
1328|
1329|    #### Default type
1330|
1331|    With the default values for @a StringType (`std::string`), the default
1332|    value for @a string_t is:
1333|
1334|    @code {.cpp}
1335|    std::string
1336|    @endcode
1337|
1338|    #### Encoding
1339|
1340|    Strings are stored in UTF-8 encoding. Therefore, functions like
1341|    `std::string::size()` or `std::string::length()` return the number of
1342|    bytes in the string rather than the number of characters or glyphs.
1343|
1344|    #### String comparison
1345|
1346|    [RFC 7159](http://rfc7159.net/rfc7159) states:
1347|    > Software implementations are typically required to test names of object
1348|    > members for equality. Implementations that transform the textual
1349|    > representation into sequences of Unicode code units and then perform the
1350|    > comparison numerically, code unit by code unit, are interoperable in the
1351|    > sense that implementations will agree in all cases on equality or
1352|    > inequality of two strings. For example, implementations that compare
1353|    > strings with escaped characters unconverted may incorrectly find that
1354|    > `"a\\b"` and `"a\u005Cb"` are not equal.
1355|
1356|    This implementation is interoperable as it does compare strings code unit
1357|    by code unit.
1358|
1359|    #### Storage
1360|
1361|    String values are stored as pointers in a @ref basic_json type. That is,
1362|    for any access to string values, a pointer of type `string_t*` must be
1363|    dereferenced.
1364|
1365|    @since version 1.0.0
1366|    */
1367|    using string_t = StringType;
1368|
1369|    /*!
1370|    @brief a type for a boolean
1371|
1372|    [RFC 7159](http://rfc7159.net/rfc7159) implicitly describes a boolean as a
1373|    type which differentiates the two literals `true` and `false`.
1374|
1375|    To store objects in C++, a type is defined by the template parameter @a
1376|    BooleanType which chooses the type to use.
1377|
1378|    #### Default type
1379|
1380|    With the default values for @a BooleanType (`bool`), the default value for
1381|    @a boolean_t is:
1382|
1383|    @code {.cpp}
1384|    bool
1385|    @endcode
1386|
1387|    #### Storage
1388|
1389|    Boolean values are stored directly inside a @ref basic_json type.
1390|
1391|    @since version 1.0.0
1392|    */
1393|    using boolean_t = BooleanType;
1394|
1395|    /*!
1396|    @brief a type for a number (integer)
1397|
1398|    [RFC 7159](http://rfc7159.net/rfc7159) describes numbers as follows:
1399|    > The representation of numbers is similar to that used in most
1400|    > programming languages. A number is represented in base 10 using decimal
1401|    > digits. It contains an integer component that may be prefixed with an
1402|    > optional minus sign, which may be followed by a fraction part and/or an
1403|    > exponent part. Leading zeros are not allowed. (...) Numeric values that
1404|    > cannot be represented in the grammar below (such as Infinity and NaN)
1405|    > are not permitted.
1406|
1407|    This description includes both integer and floating-point numbers.
1408|    However, C++ allows more precise storage if it is known whether the number
1409|    is a signed integer, an unsigned integer or a floating-point number.
1410|    Therefore, three different types, @ref number_integer_t, @ref
1411|    number_unsigned_t and @ref number_float_t are used.
1412|
1413|    To store integer numbers in C++, a type is defined by the template
1414|    parameter @a NumberIntegerType which chooses the type to use.
1415|
1416|    #### Default type
1417|
1418|    With the default values for @a NumberIntegerType (`int64_t`), the default
1419|    value for @a number_integer_t is:
1420|
1421|    @code {.cpp}
1422|    int64_t
1423|    @endcode
1424|
1425|    #### Default behavior
1426|
1427|    - The restrictions about leading zeros is not enforced in C++. Instead,
1428|      leading zeros in integer literals lead to an interpretation as octal
1429|      number. Internally, the value will be stored as decimal number. For
1430|      instance, the C++ integer literal `010` will be serialized to `8`.
1431|      During deserialization, leading zeros yield an error.
1432|    - Not-a-number (NaN) values will be serialized to `null`.
1433|
1434|    #### Limits
1435|
1436|    [RFC 7159](http://rfc7159.net/rfc7159) specifies:
1437|    > An implementation may set limits on the range and precision of numbers.
1438|
1439|    When the default type is used, the maximal integer number that can be
1440|    stored is `9223372036854775807` (INT64_MAX) and the minimal integer number
1441|    that can be stored is `-9223372036854775808` (INT64_MIN). Integer numbers
1442|    that are out of range will yield over/underflow when used in a
1443|    constructor. During deserialization, too large or small integer numbers
1444|    will be automatically be stored as @ref number_unsigned_t or @ref
1445|    number_float_t.
1446|
1447|    [RFC 7159](http://rfc7159.net/rfc7159) further states:
1448|    > Note that when such software is used, numbers that are integers and are
1449|    > in the range \f$[-2^{53}+1, 2^{53}-1]\f$ are interoperable in the sense
1450|    > that implementations will agree exactly on their numeric values.
1451|
1452|    As this range is a subrange of the exactly supported range [INT64_MIN,
1453|    INT64_MAX], this class's integer type is interoperable.
1454|
1455|    #### Storage
1456|
1457|    Integer number values are stored directly inside a @ref basic_json type.
1458|
1459|    @sa @ref number_float_t -- type for number values (floating-point)
1460|
1461|    @sa @ref number_unsigned_t -- type for number values (unsigned integer)
1462|
1463|    @since version 1.0.0
1464|    */
1465|    using number_integer_t = NumberIntegerType;
1466|
1467|    /*!
1468|    @brief a type for a number (unsigned)
1469|
1470|    [RFC 7159](http://rfc7159.net/rfc7159) describes numbers as follows:
1471|    > The representation of numbers is similar to that used in most
1472|    > programming languages. A number is represented in base 10 using decimal
1473|    > digits. It contains an integer component that may be prefixed with an
1474|    > optional minus sign, which may be followed by a fraction part and/or an
1475|    > exponent part. Leading zeros are not allowed. (...) Numeric values that
1476|    > cannot be represented in the grammar below (such as Infinity and NaN)
1477|    > are not permitted.
1478|
1479|    This description includes both integer and floating-point numbers.
1480|    However, C++ allows more precise storage if it is known whether the number
1481|    is a signed integer, an unsigned integer or a floating-point number.
1482|    Therefore, three different types, @ref number_integer_t, @ref
1483|    number_unsigned_t and @ref number_float_t are used.
1484|
1485|    To store unsigned integer numbers in C++, a type is defined by the
1486|    template parameter @a NumberUnsignedType which chooses the type to use.
1487|
1488|    #### Default type
1489|
1490|    With the default values for @a NumberUnsignedType (`uint64_t`), the
1491|    default value for @a number_unsigned_t is:
1492|
1493|    @code {.cpp}
1494|    uint64_t
1495|    @endcode
1496|
1497|    #### Default behavior
1498|
1499|    - The restrictions about leading zeros is not enforced in C++. Instead,
1500|      leading zeros in integer literals lead to an interpretation as octal
1501|      number. Internally, the value will be stored as decimal number. For
1502|      instance, the C++ integer literal `010` will be serialized to `8`.
1503|      During deserialization, leading zeros yield an error.
1504|    - Not-a-number (NaN) values will be serialized to `null`.
1505|
1506|    #### Limits
1507|
1508|    [RFC 7159](http://rfc7159.net/rfc7159) specifies:
1509|    > An implementation may set limits on the range and precision of numbers.
1510|
1511|    When the default type is used, the maximal integer number that can be
1512|    stored is `18446744073709551615` (UINT64_MAX) and the minimal integer
1513|    number that can be stored is `0`. Integer numbers that are out of range
1514|    will yield over/underflow when used in a constructor. During
1515|    deserialization, too large or small integer numbers will be automatically
1516|    be stored as @ref number_integer_t or @ref number_float_t.
1517|
1518|    [RFC 7159](http://rfc7159.net/rfc7159) further states:
1519|    > Note that when such software is used, numbers that are integers and are
1520|    > in the range \f$[-2^{53}+1, 2^{53}-1]\f$ are interoperable in the sense
1521|    > that implementations will agree exactly on their numeric values.
1522|
1523|    As this range is a subrange (when considered in conjunction with the
1524|    number_integer_t type) of the exactly supported range [0, UINT64_MAX],
1525|    this class's integer type is interoperable.
1526|
1527|    #### Storage
1528|
1529|    Integer number values are stored directly inside a @ref basic_json type.
1530|
1531|    @sa @ref number_float_t -- type for number values (floating-point)
1532|    @sa @ref number_integer_t -- type for number values (integer)
1533|
1534|    @since version 2.0.0
1535|    */
1536|    using number_unsigned_t = NumberUnsignedType;
1537|
1538|    /*!
1539|    @brief a type for a number (floating-point)
1540|
1541|    [RFC 7159](http://rfc7159.net/rfc7159) describes numbers as follows:
1542|    > The representation of numbers is similar to that used in most
1543|    > programming languages. A number is represented in base 10 using decimal
1544|    > digits. It contains an integer component that may be prefixed with an
1545|    > optional minus sign, which may be followed by a fraction part and/or an
1546|    > exponent part. Leading zeros are not allowed. (...) Numeric values that
1547|    > cannot be represented in the grammar below (such as Infinity and NaN)
1548|    > are not permitted.
1549|
1550|    This description includes both integer and floating-point numbers.
1551|    However, C++ allows more precise storage if it is known whether the number
1552|    is a signed integer, an unsigned integer or a floating-point number.
1553|    Therefore, three different types, @ref number_integer_t, @ref
1554|    number_unsigned_t and @ref number_float_t are used.
1555|
1556|    To store floating-point numbers in C++, a type is defined by the template
1557|    parameter @a NumberFloatType which chooses the type to use.
1558|
1559|    #### Default type
1560|
1561|    With the default values for @a NumberFloatType (`double`), the default
1562|    value for @a number_float_t is:
1563|
1564|    @code {.cpp}
1565|    double
1566|    @endcode
1567|
1568|    #### Default behavior
1569|
1570|    - The restrictions about leading zeros is not enforced in C++. Instead,
1571|      leading zeros in floating-point literals will be ignored. Internally,
1572|      the value will be stored as decimal number. For instance, the C++
1573|      floating-point literal `01.2` will be serialized to `1.2`. During
1574|      deserialization, leading zeros yield an error.
1575|    - Not-a-number (NaN) values will be serialized to `null`.
1576|
1577|    #### Limits
1578|
1579|    [RFC 7159](http://rfc7159.net/rfc7159) states:
1580|    > This specification allows implementations to set limits on the range and
1581|    > precision of numbers accepted. Since software that implements IEEE
1582|    > 754-2008 binary64 (double precision) numbers is generally available and
1583|    > widely used, good interoperability can be achieved by implementations
1584|    > that expect no more precision or range than these provide, in the sense
1585|    > that implementations will approximate JSON numbers within the expected
1586|    > precision.
1587|
1588|    This implementation does exactly follow this approach, as it uses double
1589|    precision floating-point numbers. Note values smaller than
1590|    `-1.79769313486232e+308` and values greater than `1.79769313486232e+308`
1591|    will be stored as NaN internally and be serialized to `null`.
1592|
1593|    #### Storage
1594|
1595|    Floating-point number values are stored directly inside a @ref basic_json
1596|    type.
1597|
1598|    @sa @ref number_integer_t -- type for number values (integer)
1599|
1600|    @sa @ref number_unsigned_t -- type for number values (unsigned integer)
1601|
1602|    @since version 1.0.0
1603|    */
1604|    using number_float_t = NumberFloatType;

1608|  private:
1609|
1610|    /// helper for exception-safe object creation
1611|    template<typename T, typename... Args>
1612|    static T* create(Args&& ... args)
1613|    {
1614|        AllocatorType<T> alloc;
1615|        auto deleter = [&](T * object)
1616|        {
1617|            alloc.deallocate(object, 1);
1618|        };
1619|        std::unique_ptr<T, decltype(deleter)> object(alloc.allocate(1), deleter);
1620|        alloc.construct(object.get(), std::forward<Args>(args)...);
1621|        assert(object != nullptr);
1622|        return object.release();
1623|    }

1628|
1629|    /*!
1630|    @brief a JSON value
1631|
1632|    The actual storage for a JSON value of the @ref basic_json class. This
1633|    union combines the different storage types for the JSON value types
1634|    defined in @ref value_t.
1635|
1636|    JSON type | value_t type    | used type
1637|    --------- | --------------- | ------------------------
1638|    object    | object          | pointer to @ref object_t
1639|    array     | array           | pointer to @ref array_t
1640|    string    | string          | pointer to @ref string_t
1641|    boolean   | boolean         | @ref boolean_t
1642|    number    | number_integer  | @ref number_integer_t
1643|    number    | number_unsigned | @ref number_unsigned_t
1644|    number    | number_float    | @ref number_float_t
1645|    null      | null            | *no value is stored*
1646|
1647|    @note Variable-length types (objects, arrays, and strings) are stored as
1648|    pointers. The size of the union should not exceed 64 bits if the default
1649|    value types are used.
1650|
1651|    @since version 1.0.0
1652|    */
1653|    union json_value
1654|    {
1655|        /// object (stored with pointer to save storage)
1656|        object_t* object;
1657|        /// array (stored with pointer to save storage)
1658|        array_t* array;
1659|        /// string (stored with pointer to save storage)
1660|        string_t* string;
1661|        /// boolean
1662|        boolean_t boolean;
1663|        /// number (integer)
1664|        number_integer_t number_integer;
1665|        /// number (unsigned integer)
1666|        number_unsigned_t number_unsigned;
1667|        /// number (floating-point)
1668|        number_float_t number_float;
1669|
1670|        /// default constructor (for null values)
1671|        json_value() = default;
1672|        /// constructor for booleans
1673|        json_value(boolean_t v) noexcept : boolean(v) {}
1674|        /// constructor for numbers (integer)
1675|        json_value(number_integer_t v) noexcept : number_integer(v) {}
1676|        /// constructor for numbers (unsigned)

1796|        object_start,
1797|        /// the parser read `}` and finished processing a JSON object

1800|        array_start,

1809|    /*!
1810|    @brief per-element parser callback type
1811|
1812|    With a parser callback function, the result of parsing a JSON text can be
1813|    influenced. When passed to @ref parse(std::istream&, const
1814|    parser_callback_t) or @ref parse(const CharT, const parser_callback_t),
1815|    it is called on certain events (passed as @ref parse_event_t via parameter
1816|    @a event) with a set recursion depth @a depth and context JSON value
1817|    @a parsed. The return value of the callback function is a boolean
1818|    indicating whether the element that emitted the callback shall be kept or
1819|    not.
1820|
1821|    We distinguish six scenarios (determined by the event type) in which the
1822|    callback function can be called. The following table describes the values
1823|    of the parameters @a depth, @a event, and @a parsed.
1824|
1825|    parameter @a event | description | parameter @a depth | parameter @a parsed
1826|    ------------------ | ----------- | ------------------ | -------------------
1827|    parse_event_t::object_start | the parser read `{` and started to process a JSON object | depth of the parent of the JSON object | a JSON value with type discarded
1828|    parse_event_t::key | the parser read a key of a value in an object | depth of the currently parsed JSON object | a JSON string containing the key
1829|    parse_event_t::object_end | the parser read `}` and finished processing a JSON object | depth of the parent of the JSON object | the parsed JSON object
1830|    parse_event_t::array_start | the parser read `[` and started to process a JSON array | depth of the parent of the JSON array | a JSON value with type discarded
1831|    parse_event_t::array_end | the parser read `]` and finished processing a JSON array | depth of the parent of the JSON array | the parsed JSON array
1832|    parse_event_t::value | the parser finished reading a JSON value | depth of the value | the parsed JSON value
1833|
1834|    @image html callback_events.png "Example when certain parse events are triggered"
1835|
1836|    Discarding a value (i.e., returning `false`) has different effects
1837|    depending on the context in which function was called:
1838|
1839|    - Discarded values in structured types are skipped. That is, the parser
1840|      will behave as if the discarded value was never read.
1841|    - In case a value outside a structured type is skipped, it is replaced
1842|      with `null`. This case happens if the top-level element is skipped.
1843|
1844|    @param[in] depth  the depth of the recursion during parsing
1845|
1846|    @param[in] event  an event of type parse_event_t indicating the context in
1847|    the callback function has been called
1848|
1849|    @param[in,out] parsed  the current intermediate parse result; note that
1850|    writing to this value has no effect for parse_event_t::key events
1851|
1852|    @return Whether the JSON value which called the function during parsing
1853|    should be kept (`true`) or not (`false`). In the latter case, it is either
1854|    skipped completely or replaced by an empty discarded object.
1855|
1856|    @sa @ref parse(std::istream&, parser_callback_t) or
1857|    @ref parse(const CharT, const parser_callback_t) for examples
1858|
1859|    @since version 1.0.0
1860|    */
1861|    using parser_callback_t = std::function<bool(int depth,
1862|                              parse_event_t event,
1863|                              basic_json& parsed)>;

1999|    /*!
2000|    @brief create a container (array or object) from an initializer list
2001|
2002|    Creates a JSON value of type array or object from the passed initializer
2003|    list @a init. In case @a type_deduction is `true` (default), the type of
2004|    the JSON value to be created is deducted from the initializer list @a init
2005|    according to the following rules:
2006|
2007|    1. If the list is empty, an empty JSON object value `{}` is created.
2008|    2. If the list consists of pairs whose first element is a string, a JSON
2009|       object value is created where the first elements of the pairs are
2010|       treated as keys and the second elements are as values.
2011|    3. In all other cases, an array is created.
2012|
2013|    The rules aim to create the best fit between a C++ initializer list and
2014|    JSON values. The rationale is as follows:
2015|
2016|    1. The empty initializer list is written as `{}` which is exactly an empty
2017|       JSON object.
2018|    2. C++ has now way of describing mapped types other than to list a list of
2019|       pairs. As JSON requires that keys must be of type string, rule 2 is the
2020|       weakest constraint one can pose on initializer lists to interpret them
2021|       as an object.
2022|    3. In all other cases, the initializer list could not be interpreted as
2023|       JSON object type, so interpreting it as JSON array type is safe.
2024|
2025|    With the rules described above, the following JSON values cannot be
2026|    expressed by an initializer list:
2027|
2028|    - the empty array (`[]`): use @ref array(std::initializer_list<basic_json>)
2029|      with an empty initializer list in this case
2030|    - arrays whose elements satisfy rule 2: use @ref
2031|      array(std::initializer_list<basic_json>) with the same initializer list
2032|      in this case
2033|
2034|    @note When used without parentheses around an empty initializer list, @ref
2035|    basic_json() is called instead of this function, yielding the JSON null
2036|    value.
2037|
2038|    @param[in] init  initializer list with JSON values
2039|
2040|    @param[in] type_deduction internal parameter; when set to `true`, the type
2041|    of the JSON value is deducted from the initializer list @a init; when set
2042|    to `false`, the type provided via @a manual_type is forced. This mode is
2043|    used by the functions @ref array(std::initializer_list<basic_json>) and
2044|    @ref object(std::initializer_list<basic_json>).
2045|
2046|    @param[in] manual_type internal parameter; when @a type_deduction is set
2047|    to `false`, the created JSON value will use the provided type (only @ref
2048|    value_t::array and @ref value_t::object are valid); when @a type_deduction
2049|    is set to `true`, this parameter has no effect
2050|
2051|    @throw std::domain_error if @a type_deduction is `false`, @a manual_type
2052|    is `value_t::object`, but @a init contains an element which is not a pair
2053|    whose first element is a string; example: `"cannot create object from
2054|    initializer list"`
2055|
2056|    @complexity Linear in the size of the initializer list @a init.
2057|
2058|    @liveexample{The example below shows how JSON values are created from
2059|    initializer lists.,basic_json__list_init_t}
2060|
2061|    @sa @ref array(std::initializer_list<basic_json>) -- create a JSON array
2062|    value from an initializer list
2063|    @sa @ref object(std::initializer_list<basic_json>) -- create a JSON object
2064|    value from an initializer list
2065|
2066|    @since version 1.0.0
2067|    */
2068|    basic_json(std::initializer_list<basic_json> init,
2069|               bool type_deduction = true,
2070|               value_t manual_type = value_t::array)
2071|    {
2072|        // check if each element is an array with two elements whose first
2073|        // element is a string
2074|        bool is_an_object = std::all_of(init.begin(), init.end(),
2075|                                        [](const basic_json & element)
2076|        {
2077|            return element.is_array() and element.size() == 2 and element[0].is_string();
2078|        });
2079|
2080|        // adjust type if type deduction is not wanted
2081|        if (not type_deduction)
2082|        {
2083|            // if array is wanted, do not create an object though possible
2084|            if (manual_type == value_t::array)
2085|            {
2086|                is_an_object = false;
2087|            }
2088|
2089|            // if object is wanted but impossible, throw an exception
2090|            if (manual_type == value_t::object and not is_an_object)
2091|            {
2092|                JSON_THROW(std::domain_error("cannot create object from initializer list"));
2093|            }
2094|        }
2095|
2096|        if (is_an_object)
2097|        {
2098|            // the initializer list is a list of pairs -> create object
2099|            m_type = value_t::object;
2100|            m_value = value_t::object;
2101|
2102|            std::for_each(init.begin(), init.end(), [this](const basic_json & element)
2103|            {
2104|                m_value.object->emplace(*(element[0].m_value.string), element[1]);
2105|            });
2106|        }
2107|        else
2108|        {
2109|            // the initializer list describes an array -> create array
2110|            m_type = value_t::array;
2111|            m_value.array = create<array_t>(init);
2112|        }
2113|
2114|        assert_invariant();
2115|    }

5812|    /*!
5813|    @brief comparison: equal
5814|
5815|    Compares two JSON values for equality according to the following rules:
5816|    - Two JSON values are equal if (1) they are from the same type and (2)
5817|      their stored values are the same.
5818|    - Integer and floating-point numbers are automatically converted before
5819|      comparison. Floating-point numbers are compared indirectly: two
5820|      floating-point numbers `f1` and `f2` are considered equal if neither
5821|      `f1 > f2` nor `f2 > f1` holds.
5822|    - Two JSON null values are equal.
5823|
5824|    @param[in] lhs  first JSON value to consider
5825|    @param[in] rhs  second JSON value to consider
5826|    @return whether the values @a lhs and @a rhs are equal
5827|
5828|    @complexity Linear.
5829|
5830|    @liveexample{The example demonstrates comparing several JSON
5831|    types.,operator__equal}
5832|
5833|    @since version 1.0.0
5834|    */
5835|    friend bool operator==(const_reference lhs, const_reference rhs) noexcept
5836|    {
5837|        const auto lhs_type = lhs.type();
5838|        const auto rhs_type = rhs.type();
5839|
5840|        if (lhs_type == rhs_type)
5841|        {
5842|            switch (lhs_type)
5843|            {
5844|                case value_t::array:
5845|                {
5846|                    return *lhs.m_value.array == *rhs.m_value.array;
5847|                }
5848|                case value_t::object:
5849|                {
5850|                    return *lhs.m_value.object == *rhs.m_value.object;
5851|                }
5852|                case value_t::null:
5853|                {
5854|                    return true;
5855|                }
5856|                case value_t::string:
5857|                {
5858|                    return *lhs.m_value.string == *rhs.m_value.string;
5859|                }
5860|                case value_t::boolean:
5861|                {
5862|                    return lhs.m_value.boolean == rhs.m_value.boolean;
5863|                }
5864|                case value_t::number_integer:
5865|                {
5866|                    return lhs.m_value.number_integer == rhs.m_value.number_integer;
5867|                }
5868|                case value_t::number_unsigned:
5869|                {
5870|                    return lhs.m_value.number_unsigned == rhs.m_value.number_unsigned;
5871|                }
5872|                case value_t::number_float:
5873|                {
5874|                    return lhs.m_value.number_float == rhs.m_value.number_float;
5875|                }
5876|                default:
5877|                {
5878|                    return false;
5879|                }
5880|            }
5881|        }
5882|        else if (lhs_type == value_t::number_integer and rhs_type == value_t::number_float)
5883|        {
5884|            return static_cast<number_float_t>(lhs.m_value.number_integer) == rhs.m_value.number_float;
5885|        }
5886|        else if (lhs_type == value_t::number_float and rhs_type == value_t::number_integer)
5887|        {
5888|            return lhs.m_value.number_float == static_cast<number_float_t>(rhs.m_value.number_integer);
5889|        }
5890|        else if (lhs_type == value_t::number_unsigned and rhs_type == value_t::number_float)
5891|        {
5892|            return static_cast<number_float_t>(lhs.m_value.number_unsigned) == rhs.m_value.number_float;
5893|        }
5894|        else if (lhs_type == value_t::number_float and rhs_type == value_t::number_unsigned)
5895|        {
5896|            return lhs.m_value.number_float == static_cast<number_float_t>(rhs.m_value.number_unsigned);
5897|        }
5898|        else if (lhs_type == value_t::number_unsigned and rhs_type == value_t::number_integer)
5899|        {
5900|            return static_cast<number_integer_t>(lhs.m_value.number_unsigned) == rhs.m_value.number_integer;
5901|        }
5902|        else if (lhs_type == value_t::number_integer and rhs_type == value_t::number_unsigned)

5905|        }
5906|

6173|        /*!

6210|                        const auto new_indent = current_indent + indent_step;

6215|

6217|                        auto i = val.m_value.object->cbegin();

6243|
6244|                        // first n-1 elements

6265|                    return;
6266|                }
6267|
6268|                case value_t::array:
6269|                {

6274|                    }
6275|
6276|                    if (pretty_print)

6286|

6288|                        for (auto i = val.m_value.array->cbegin(); i != val.m_value.array->cend() - 1; ++i)
6289|                        {

6291|                            dump(*i, true, indent_step, new_indent);
6292|                            o.write(",\n", 2);
6293|                        }
6294|

6299|
6300|                        o.put('\n');
6301|                        o.write(indent_string.c_str(), current_indent);
6302|                        o.put(']');

6304|                    else
6305|                    {
6306|                        o.put('[');
6307|
6308|                        // first n-1 elements
6309|                        for (auto i = val.m_value.array->cbegin(); i != val.m_value.array->cend() - 1; ++i)
6310|                        {
6311|                            dump(*i, false, indent_step, current_indent);
6312|                            o.put(',');
6313|                        }
6314|
6315|                        // last element
6316|                        assert(not val.m_value.array->empty());

6319|                        o.put(']');

6322|                    return;
6323|                }
6324|
6325|                case value_t::string:

6340|                    {

6350|                }

6356|                }

6358|                case value_t::number_float:

6378|      private:
6379|        /*!
6380|        @brief calculates the extra space to escape a JSON string
6381|
6382|        @param[in] s  the string to escape
6383|        @return the number of characters required to escape string @a s
6384|
6385|        @complexity Linear in the length of string @a s.
6386|        */
6387|        static std::size_t extra_space(const string_t& s) noexcept
6388|        {
6389|            return std::accumulate(s.begin(), s.end(), size_t{},
6390|                                   [](size_t res, typename string_t::value_type c)
6391|            {
6392|                switch (c)
6393|                {
6394|                    case '"':
6395|                    case '\\':
6396|                    case '\b':
6397|                    case '\f':
6398|                    case '\n':
6399|                    case '\r':
6400|                    case '\t':
6401|                    {
6402|                        // from c (1 byte) to \x (2 bytes)
6403|                        return res + 1;
6404|                    }
6405|
6406|                    case 0x00:
6407|                    case 0x01:
6408|                    case 0x02:
6409|                    case 0x03:
6410|                    case 0x04:
6411|                    case 0x05:
6412|                    case 0x06:
6413|                    case 0x07:
6414|                    case 0x0b:
6415|                    case 0x0e:
6416|                    case 0x0f:
6417|                    case 0x10:
6418|                    case 0x11:
6419|                    case 0x12:
6420|                    case 0x13:
6421|                    case 0x14:
6422|                    case 0x15:
6423|                    case 0x16:
6424|                    case 0x17:
6425|                    case 0x18:
6426|                    case 0x19:
6427|                    case 0x1a:
6428|                    case 0x1b:
6429|                    case 0x1c:
6430|                    case 0x1d:
6431|                    case 0x1e:
6432|                    case 0x1f:
6433|                    {
6434|                        // from c (1 byte) to \uxxxx (6 bytes)
6435|                        return res + 5;
6436|                    }
6437|
6438|                    default:
6439|                    {
6440|                        return res;
6441|                    }
6442|                }
6443|            });
6444|        }
6445|
6446|        /*!
6447|        @brief dump escaped string
6448|
6449|        Escape a string by replacing certain special characters by a sequence
6450|        of an escape character (backslash) and another character and other
6451|        control characters by a sequence of "\u" followed by a four-digit hex
6452|        representation. The escaped string is written to output stream @a o.
6453|
6454|        @param[in] s  the string to escape
6455|
6456|        @complexity Linear in the length of string @a s.
6457|        */
6458|        void dump_escaped(const string_t& s) const
6459|        {
6460|            const auto space = extra_space(s);
6461|            if (space == 0)
6462|            {
6463|                o.write(s.c_str(), static_cast<std::streamsize>(s.size()));
6464|                return;
6465|            }
6466|
6467|            // create a result string of necessary size
6468|            string_t result(s.size() + space, '\\');
6469|            std::size_t pos = 0;
6470|
6471|            for (const auto& c : s)
6472|            {
6473|                switch (c)
6474|                {
6475|                    // quotation mark (0x22)
6476|                    case '"':
6477|                    {
6478|                        result[pos + 1] = '"';
6479|                        pos += 2;
6480|                        break;
6481|                    }
6482|
6483|                    // reverse solidus (0x5c)
6484|                    case '\\':
6485|                    {
6486|                        // nothing to change
6487|                        pos += 2;
6488|                        break;
6489|                    }
6490|
6491|                    // backspace (0x08)
6492|                    case '\b':
6493|                    {
6494|                        result[pos + 1] = 'b';
6495|                        pos += 2;
6496|                        break;
6497|                    }
6498|
6499|                    // formfeed (0x0c)
6500|                    case '\f':
6501|                    {
6502|                        result[pos + 1] = 'f';
6503|                        pos += 2;
6504|                        break;
6505|                    }
6506|
6507|                    // newline (0x0a)
6508|                    case '\n':
6509|                    {
6510|                        result[pos + 1] = 'n';
6511|                        pos += 2;
6512|                        break;
6513|                    }
6514|
6515|                    // carriage return (0x0d)
6516|                    case '\r':
6517|                    {
6518|                        result[pos + 1] = 'r';
6519|                        pos += 2;
6520|                        break;
6521|                    }
6522|
6523|                    // horizontal tab (0x09)
6524|                    case '\t':
6525|                    {
6526|                        result[pos + 1] = 't';
6527|                        pos += 2;
6528|                        break;
6529|                    }
6530|
6531|                    case 0x00:
6532|                    case 0x01:
6533|                    case 0x02:
6534|                    case 0x03:
6535|                    case 0x04:
6536|                    case 0x05:
6537|                    case 0x06:
6538|                    case 0x07:
6539|                    case 0x0b:
6540|                    case 0x0e:
6541|                    case 0x0f:
6542|                    case 0x10:
6543|                    case 0x11:
6544|                    case 0x12:
6545|                    case 0x13:
6546|                    case 0x14:
6547|                    case 0x15:
6548|                    case 0x16:
6549|                    case 0x17:
6550|                    case 0x18:
6551|                    case 0x19:
6552|                    case 0x1a:
6553|                    case 0x1b:
6554|                    case 0x1c:
6555|                    case 0x1d:
6556|                    case 0x1e:
6557|                    case 0x1f:
6558|                    {
6559|                        // convert a number 0..15 to its hex representation
6560|                        // (0..f)
6561|                        static const char hexify[16] =
6562|                        {
6563|                            '0', '1', '2', '3', '4', '5', '6', '7',
6564|                            '8', '9', 'a', 'b', 'c', 'd', 'e', 'f'
6565|                        };
6566|
6567|                        // print character c as \uxxxx
6568|                        for (const char m :
6569|                    { 'u', '0', '0', hexify[c >> 4], hexify[c & 0x0f]
6570|                        })
6571|                        {
6572|                            result[++pos] = m;
6573|                        }
6574|
6575|                        ++pos;
6576|                        break;
6577|                    }
6578|
6579|                    default:
6580|                    {
6581|                        // all other characters are added as-is
6582|                        result[pos++] = c;
6583|                        break;
6584|                    }
6585|                }
6586|            }
6587|
6588|            assert(pos == s.size() + space);
6589|            o.write(result.c_str(), static_cast<std::streamsize>(result.size()));
6590|        }

6592|        /*!
6593|        @brief dump an integer
6594|
6595|        Dump a given integer to output stream @a o. Works internally with
6596|        @a number_buffer.
6597|
6598|        @param[in] x  integer number (signed or unsigned) to dump
6599|        @tparam NumberType either @a number_integer_t or @a number_unsigned_t
6600|        */
6601|        template<typename NumberType, detail::enable_if_t <
6602|                     std::is_same<NumberType, number_unsigned_t>::value or
6603|                     std::is_same<NumberType, number_integer_t>::value, int> = 0>
6604|        void dump_integer(NumberType x)
6605|        {
6606|            // special case for "0"
6607|            if (x == 0)
6608|            {
6609|                o.put('0');
6610|                return;
6611|            }
6612|
6613|            const bool is_negative = x < 0;
6614|            size_t i = 0;
6615|
6616|            // spare 1 byte for '\0'
6617|            while (x != 0 and i < number_buffer.size() - 1)
6618|            {
6619|                const auto digit = std::labs(static_cast<long>(x % 10));
6620|                number_buffer[i++] = static_cast<char>('0' + digit);
6621|                x /= 10;
6622|            }
6623|
6624|            // make sure the number has been processed completely
6625|            assert(x == 0);
6626|
6627|            if (is_negative)
6628|            {
6629|                // make sure there is capacity for the '-'
6630|                assert(i < number_buffer.size() - 2);
6631|                number_buffer[i++] = '-';
6632|            }
6633|
6634|            std::reverse(number_buffer.begin(), number_buffer.begin() + i);
6635|            o.write(number_buffer.data(), static_cast<std::streamsize>(i));
6636|        }
6637|
6638|        /*!
6639|        @brief dump a floating-point number
6640|
6641|        Dump a given floating-point number to output stream @a o. Works
6642|        internally with @a number_buffer.
6643|
6644|        @param[in] x  floating-point number to dump
6645|        */
6646|        void dump_float(number_float_t x)
6647|        {
6648|            // NaN / inf
6649|            if (not std::isfinite(x) or std::isnan(x))
6650|            {
6651|                o.write("null", 4);
6652|                return;
6653|            }
6654|
6655|            // special case for 0.0 and -0.0
6656|            if (x == 0)
6657|            {
6658|                if (std::signbit(x))
6659|                {
6660|                    o.write("-0.0", 4);
6661|                }
6662|                else
6663|                {
6664|                    o.write("0.0", 3);
6665|                }
6666|                return;
6667|            }
6668|
6669|            // get number of digits for a text -> float -> text round-trip
6670|            static constexpr auto d = std::numeric_limits<number_float_t>::digits10;
6671|
6672|            // the actual conversion
6673|            long len = snprintf(number_buffer.data(), number_buffer.size(),
6674|                                "%.*g", d, x);
6675|
6676|            // negative value indicates an error
6677|            assert(len > 0);
6678|            // check if buffer was large enough
6679|            assert(static_cast<size_t>(len) < number_buffer.size());
6680|
6681|            // erase thousands separator
6682|            if (thousands_sep != '\0')
6683|            {
6684|                const auto end = std::remove(number_buffer.begin(),
6685|                                             number_buffer.begin() + len,
6686|                                             thousands_sep);
6687|                std::fill(end, number_buffer.end(), '\0');
6688|                assert((end - number_buffer.begin()) <= len);
6689|                len = (end - number_buffer.begin());
6690|            }
6691|
6692|            // convert decimal point to '.'
6693|            if (decimal_point != '\0' and decimal_point != '.')
6694|            {
6695|                for (auto& c : number_buffer)
6696|                {
6697|                    if (c == decimal_point)
6698|                    {
6699|                        c = '.';
6700|                        break;
6701|                    }
6702|                }
6703|            }
6704|
6705|            o.write(number_buffer.data(), static_cast<std::streamsize>(len));
6706|
6707|            // determine if need to append ".0"
6708|            const bool value_is_int_like = std::none_of(number_buffer.begin(),
6709|                                           number_buffer.begin() + len + 1,
6710|                                           [](char c)
6711|            {
6712|                return c == '.' or c == 'e';
6713|            });
6714|
6715|            if (value_is_int_like)
6716|            {
6717|                o.write(".0", 2);
6718|            }
6719|        }

6721|      private:
6722|        /// the output of the serializer
6723|        std::ostream& o;
6724|
6725|        /// a (hopefully) large enough character buffer
6726|        std::array<char, 64> number_buffer{{}};
6727|
6728|        /// the locale
6729|        const std::lconv* loc = nullptr;
6730|        /// the locale's thousand separator character
6731|        const char thousands_sep = '\0';
6732|        /// the locale's decimal point character
6733|        const char decimal_point = '\0';
6734|
6735|        /// the indentation string
6736|        string_t indent_string = string_t(512, ' ');
6737|    };

6907|    /*!
6908|    @brief deserialize from an iterator range with contiguous storage
6909|
6910|    This function reads from an iterator range of a container with contiguous
6911|    storage of 1-byte values. Compatible container types include
6912|    `std::vector`, `std::string`, `std::array`, `std::valarray`, and
6913|    `std::initializer_list`. Furthermore, C-style arrays can be used with
6914|    `std::begin()`/`std::end()`. User-defined containers can be used as long
6915|    as they implement random-access iterators and a contiguous storage.
6916|
6917|    @pre The iterator range is contiguous. Violating this precondition yields
6918|    undefined behavior. **This precondition is enforced with an assertion.**
6919|    @pre Each element in the range has a size of 1 byte. Violating this
6920|    precondition yields undefined behavior. **This precondition is enforced
6921|    with a static assertion.**
6922|
6923|    @warning There is no way to enforce all preconditions at compile-time. If
6924|             the function is called with noncompliant iterators and with
6925|             assertions switched off, the behavior is undefined and will most
6926|             likely yield segmentation violation.
6927|
6928|    @tparam IteratorType iterator of container with contiguous storage
6929|    @param[in] first  begin of the range to parse (included)
6930|    @param[in] last  end of the range to parse (excluded)
6931|    @param[in] cb  a parser callback function of type @ref parser_callback_t
6932|    which is used to control the deserialization by filtering unwanted values
6933|    (optional)
6934|
6935|    @return result of the deserialization
6936|
6937|    @complexity Linear in the length of the input. The parser is a predictive
6938|    LL(1) parser. The complexity can be higher if the parser callback function
6939|    @a cb has a super-linear complexity.
6940|
6941|    @note A UTF-8 byte order mark is silently ignored.
6942|
6943|    @liveexample{The example below demonstrates the `parse()` function reading
6944|    from an iterator range.,parse__iteratortype__parser_callback_t}
6945|
6946|    @since version 2.0.3
6947|    */
6948|    template<class IteratorType, typename std::enable_if<
6949|                 std::is_base_of<
6950|                     std::random_access_iterator_tag,
6951|                     typename std::iterator_traits<IteratorType>::iterator_category>::value, int>::type = 0>
6952|    static basic_json parse(IteratorType first, IteratorType last,
6953|                            const parser_callback_t cb = nullptr)
6954|    {
6955|        // assertion to check that the iterator range is indeed contiguous,
6956|        // see http://stackoverflow.com/a/35008842/266378 for more discussion
6957|        assert(std::accumulate(first, last, std::pair<bool, int>(true, 0),
6958|                               [&first](std::pair<bool, int> res, decltype(*first) val)
6959|        {
6960|            res.first &= (val == *(std::next(std::addressof(*first), res.second++)));
6961|            return res;
6962|        }).first);
6963|
6964|        // assertion to check that each element is 1 byte long
6965|        static_assert(sizeof(typename std::iterator_traits<IteratorType>::value_type) == 1,
6966|                      "each element in the iterator range must have the size of 1 byte");
6967|
6968|        // if iterator range is empty, create a parser with an empty string
6969|        // to generate "unexpected EOF" error message
6970|        if (std::distance(first, last) <= 0)
6971|        {
6972|            return parser("").parse();
6973|        }
6974|
6975|        return parser(first, last, cb).parse();
6976|    }

7080|    /*!
7081|    @note Some code in the switch cases has been copied, because otherwise
7082|          copilers would complain about implicit fallthrough and there is no
7083|          portable attribute to mute such warnings.
7084|    */
7085|    template<typename T>
7086|    static void add_to_vector(std::vector<uint8_t>& vec, size_t bytes, const T number)
7087|    {
7088|        assert(bytes == 1 or bytes == 2 or bytes == 4 or bytes == 8);
7089|
7090|        switch (bytes)
7091|        {
7092|            case 8:
7093|            {
7094|                vec.push_back(static_cast<uint8_t>((static_cast<uint64_t>(number) >> 070) & 0xff));
7095|                vec.push_back(static_cast<uint8_t>((static_cast<uint64_t>(number) >> 060) & 0xff));
7096|                vec.push_back(static_cast<uint8_t>((static_cast<uint64_t>(number) >> 050) & 0xff));
7097|                vec.push_back(static_cast<uint8_t>((static_cast<uint64_t>(number) >> 040) & 0xff));
7098|                vec.push_back(static_cast<uint8_t>((number >> 030) & 0xff));
7099|                vec.push_back(static_cast<uint8_t>((number >> 020) & 0xff));
7100|                vec.push_back(static_cast<uint8_t>((number >> 010) & 0xff));
7101|                vec.push_back(static_cast<uint8_t>(number & 0xff));
7102|                break;
7103|            }
7104|
7105|            case 4:
7106|            {
7107|                vec.push_back(static_cast<uint8_t>((number >> 030) & 0xff));
7108|                vec.push_back(static_cast<uint8_t>((number >> 020) & 0xff));
7109|                vec.push_back(static_cast<uint8_t>((number >> 010) & 0xff));
7110|                vec.push_back(static_cast<uint8_t>(number & 0xff));
7111|                break;
7112|            }
7113|
7114|            case 2:
7115|            {
7116|                vec.push_back(static_cast<uint8_t>((number >> 010) & 0xff));
7117|                vec.push_back(static_cast<uint8_t>(number & 0xff));
7118|                break;
7119|            }
7120|
7121|            case 1:
7122|            {
7123|                vec.push_back(static_cast<uint8_t>(number & 0xff));
7124|                break;
7125|            }
7126|        }
7127|    }

7129|    /*!
7130|    @brief take sufficient bytes from a vector to fill an integer variable
7131|
7132|    In the context of binary serialization formats, we need to read several
7133|    bytes from a byte vector and combine them to multi-byte integral data
7134|    types.
7135|
7136|    @param[in] vec  byte vector to read from
7137|    @param[in] current_index  the position in the vector after which to read
7138|
7139|    @return the next sizeof(T) bytes from @a vec, in reverse order as T
7140|
7141|    @tparam T the integral return type
7142|
7143|    @throw std::out_of_range if there are less than sizeof(T)+1 bytes in the
7144|           vector @a vec to read
7145|
7146|    In the for loop, the bytes from the vector are copied in reverse order into
7147|    the return value. In the figures below, let sizeof(T)=4 and `i` be the loop
7148|    variable.
7149|
7150|    Precondition:
7151|
7152|    vec:   |   |   | a | b | c | d |      T: |   |   |   |   |
7153|                 ^               ^             ^                ^
7154|           current_index         i            ptr        sizeof(T)
7155|
7156|    Postcondition:
7157|
7158|    vec:   |   |   | a | b | c | d |      T: | d | c | b | a |
7159|                 ^   ^                                     ^
7160|                 |   i                                    ptr
7161|           current_index
7162|
7163|    @sa Code adapted from <http://stackoverflow.com/a/41031865/266378>.
7164|    */
7165|    template<typename T>
7166|    static T get_from_vector(const std::vector<uint8_t>& vec, const size_t current_index)
7167|    {
7168|        if (current_index + sizeof(T) + 1 > vec.size())
7169|        {
7170|            JSON_THROW(std::out_of_range("cannot read " + std::to_string(sizeof(T)) + " bytes from vector"));
7171|        }
7172|
7173|        T result;
7174|        auto* ptr = reinterpret_cast<uint8_t*>(&result);
7175|        for (size_t i = 0; i < sizeof(T); ++i)
7176|        {
7177|            *ptr++ = vec[current_index + sizeof(T) - i];
7178|        }
7179|        return result;
7180|    }

7182|    /*!
7183|    @brief create a MessagePack serialization of a given JSON value
7184|
7185|    This is a straightforward implementation of the MessagePack specification.
7186|
7187|    @param[in] j  JSON value to serialize
7188|    @param[in,out] v  byte vector to write the serialization to
7189|
7190|    @sa https://github.com/msgpack/msgpack/blob/master/spec.md
7191|    */
7192|    static void to_msgpack_internal(const basic_json& j, std::vector<uint8_t>& v)
7193|    {
7194|        switch (j.type())
7195|        {
7196|            case value_t::null:
7197|            {
7198|                // nil
7199|                v.push_back(0xc0);
7200|                break;
7201|            }
7202|
7203|            case value_t::boolean:
7204|            {
7205|                // true and false
7206|                v.push_back(j.m_value.boolean ? 0xc3 : 0xc2);
7207|                break;
7208|            }
7209|
7210|            case value_t::number_integer:
7211|            {
7212|                if (j.m_value.number_integer >= 0)
7213|                {
7214|                    // MessagePack does not differentiate between positive
7215|                    // signed integers and unsigned integers. Therefore, we
7216|                    // used the code from the value_t::number_unsigned case
7217|                    // here.
7218|                    if (j.m_value.number_unsigned < 128)
7219|                    {
7220|                        // positive fixnum
7221|                        add_to_vector(v, 1, j.m_value.number_unsigned);
7222|                    }
7223|                    else if (j.m_value.number_unsigned <= std::numeric_limits<uint8_t>::max())
7224|                    {
7225|                        // uint 8
7226|                        v.push_back(0xcc);
7227|                        add_to_vector(v, 1, j.m_value.number_unsigned);
7228|                    }
7229|                    else if (j.m_value.number_unsigned <= std::numeric_limits<uint16_t>::max())
7230|                    {
7231|                        // uint 16
7232|                        v.push_back(0xcd);
7233|                        add_to_vector(v, 2, j.m_value.number_unsigned);
7234|                    }
7235|                    else if (j.m_value.number_unsigned <= std::numeric_limits<uint32_t>::max())
7236|                    {
7237|                        // uint 32
7238|                        v.push_back(0xce);
7239|                        add_to_vector(v, 4, j.m_value.number_unsigned);
7240|                    }
7241|                    else if (j.m_value.number_unsigned <= std::numeric_limits<uint64_t>::max())
7242|                    {
7243|                        // uint 64
7244|                        v.push_back(0xcf);
7245|                        add_to_vector(v, 8, j.m_value.number_unsigned);
7246|                    }
7247|                }
7248|                else
7249|                {
7250|                    if (j.m_value.number_integer >= -32)
7251|                    {
7252|                        // negative fixnum
7253|                        add_to_vector(v, 1, j.m_value.number_integer);
7254|                    }
7255|                    else if (j.m_value.number_integer >= std::numeric_limits<int8_t>::min() and j.m_value.number_integer <= std::numeric_limits<int8_t>::max())
7256|                    {
7257|                        // int 8
7258|                        v.push_back(0xd0);
7259|                        add_to_vector(v, 1, j.m_value.number_integer);
7260|                    }
7261|                    else if (j.m_value.number_integer >= std::numeric_limits<int16_t>::min() and j.m_value.number_integer <= std::numeric_limits<int16_t>::max())
7262|                    {
7263|                        // int 16
7264|                        v.push_back(0xd1);
7265|                        add_to_vector(v, 2, j.m_value.number_integer);
7266|                    }
7267|                    else if (j.m_value.number_integer >= std::numeric_limits<int32_t>::min() and j.m_value.number_integer <= std::numeric_limits<int32_t>::max())
7268|                    {
7269|                        // int 32
7270|                        v.push_back(0xd2);
7271|                        add_to_vector(v, 4, j.m_value.number_integer);
7272|                    }
7273|                    else if (j.m_value.number_integer >= std::numeric_limits<int64_t>::min() and j.m_value.number_integer <= std::numeric_limits<int64_t>::max())
7274|                    {
7275|                        // int 64
7276|                        v.push_back(0xd3);
7277|                        add_to_vector(v, 8, j.m_value.number_integer);
7278|                    }
7279|                }
7280|                break;
7281|            }
7282|
7283|            case value_t::number_unsigned:
7284|            {
7285|                if (j.m_value.number_unsigned < 128)
7286|                {
7287|                    // positive fixnum
7288|                    add_to_vector(v, 1, j.m_value.number_unsigned);
7289|                }
7290|                else if (j.m_value.number_unsigned <= std::numeric_limits<uint8_t>::max())
7291|                {
7292|                    // uint 8
7293|                    v.push_back(0xcc);
7294|                    add_to_vector(v, 1, j.m_value.number_unsigned);
7295|                }
7296|                else if (j.m_value.number_unsigned <= std::numeric_limits<uint16_t>::max())
7297|                {
7298|                    // uint 16
7299|                    v.push_back(0xcd);
7300|                    add_to_vector(v, 2, j.m_value.number_unsigned);
7301|                }
7302|                else if (j.m_value.number_unsigned <= std::numeric_limits<uint32_t>::max())
7303|                {
7304|                    // uint 32
7305|                    v.push_back(0xce);
7306|                    add_to_vector(v, 4, j.m_value.number_unsigned);
7307|                }
7308|                else if (j.m_value.number_unsigned <= std::numeric_limits<uint64_t>::max())
7309|                {
7310|                    // uint 64
7311|                    v.push_back(0xcf);
7312|                    add_to_vector(v, 8, j.m_value.number_unsigned);
7313|                }
7314|                break;
7315|            }
7316|
7317|            case value_t::number_float:
7318|            {
7319|                // float 64
7320|                v.push_back(0xcb);
7321|                const auto* helper = reinterpret_cast<const uint8_t*>(&(j.m_value.number_float));
7322|                for (size_t i = 0; i < 8; ++i)
7323|                {
7324|                    v.push_back(helper[7 - i]);
7325|                }
7326|                break;
7327|            }
7328|
7329|            case value_t::string:
7330|            {
7331|                const auto N = j.m_value.string->size();
7332|                if (N <= 31)
7333|                {
7334|                    // fixstr
7335|                    v.push_back(static_cast<uint8_t>(0xa0 | N));
7336|                }
7337|                else if (N <= 255)
7338|                {
7339|                    // str 8
7340|                    v.push_back(0xd9);
7341|                    add_to_vector(v, 1, N);
7342|                }
7343|                else if (N <= 65535)
7344|                {
7345|                    // str 16
7346|                    v.push_back(0xda);
7347|                    add_to_vector(v, 2, N);
7348|                }
7349|                else if (N <= 4294967295)
7350|                {
7351|                    // str 32
7352|                    v.push_back(0xdb);
7353|                    add_to_vector(v, 4, N);
7354|                }
7355|
7356|                // append string

7693|    /*
7694|    @brief checks if given lengths do not exceed the size of a given vector
7695|
7696|    To secure the access to the byte vector during CBOR/MessagePack
7697|    deserialization, bytes are copied from the vector into buffers. This
7698|    function checks if the number of bytes to copy (@a len) does not exceed
7699|    the size @s size of the vector. Additionally, an @a offset is given from
7700|    where to start reading the bytes.
7701|
7702|    This function checks whether reading the bytes is safe; that is, offset is
7703|    a valid index in the vector, offset+len
7704|
7705|    @param[in] size    size of the byte vector
7706|    @param[in] len     number of bytes to read
7707|    @param[in] offset  offset where to start reading
7708|
7709|    vec:  x x x x x X X X X X
7710|          ^         ^         ^
7711|          0         offset    len
7712|
7713|    @throws out_of_range if `len > v.size()`
7714|    */
7715|    static void check_length(const size_t size, const size_t len, const size_t offset)
7716|    {
7717|        // simple case: requested length is greater than the vector's length
7718|        if (len > size or offset > size)
7719|        {
7720|            JSON_THROW(std::out_of_range("len out of range"));
7721|        }
7722|
7723|        // second case: adding offset would result in overflow
7724|        if ((size > (std::numeric_limits<size_t>::max() - offset)))
7725|        {
7726|            JSON_THROW(std::out_of_range("len+offset out of range"));
7727|        }
7728|
7729|        // last case: reading past the end of the vector
7730|        if (len + offset > size)
7731|        {
7732|            JSON_THROW(std::out_of_range("len+offset out of range"));
7733|        }
7734|    }

7741|

7743|    - 0xd9: str 8
7744|    - 0xda: str 16
7745|    - 0xdb: str 32
